title: שבחת בריה דר' חנינא

paragraphs: Shivhat, son of R' Hanina; another version has son of Ravina. He died because he cut down a fig tree before its time. Bava Batra 26a: R' Hanina said, ‘Shivhat beri died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time.’ Rashi explains: ‘Shivhat beri’ was his name. One may therefore say Rashi meant to prevent interpreting him as R' Hanina's son: although he said ‘Shivhat beri died,’ Rashi excluded that reading by saying ‘Shivhat beri was his name.’ There appears to be proof for Rashi, that he was not R' Hanina's son but named Shivhat Beri, from Yesh Nohalin, Bava Batra 126b: a man came before R' Hanina and said, ‘I know this man is a firstborn.’ He asked, ‘How do you know?’ He answered, ‘When people with eye trouble came to his father, he told them, “Go to Shivhat beri, for he is a firstborn and his saliva heals.”’ End quotation. How could R' Hanina happen to say ‘Shivhat beri,’ meaning ‘my son,’ and his father likewise say ‘Go to Shivhat beri,’ meaning ‘my son,’ both taking the same expression beri without either saying ‘Shivhat beni,’ as the whole Talmud ordinarily says beni? Rashi therefore explains that Shivhat Beri was his name, not R' Hanina's son. Rashbam, however, writes: ‘Shivhat beri is the firstborn's name, not the son of R' Hanina who is mentioned in Lo Yahpor, where R' Hanina said “Shivhat beri died,”’ etc. His wording implies that the Shivhat of Lo Yahpor was R' Hanina's son, beri meaning ‘my son.’ He infers this because otherwise he should have said, ‘Go to Shivhat Beri, my son,’ since there could be many Shivhats in the market; rather, beri means ‘my son.’ In my view, however, Shivhat Beri was his name, and the Lo Yahpor and Yesh Nohalin figures are all one. You, a student of the academy, may draw near to what pleases your palate.
